Its range is wide, from a deep, low bass to a clear, penetrating top, a noticeable span. Because of its frets, the strings allow fine changes of pitch and subtle shifts of colour, with an expressiveness close to the human voice. The body resonates in its own way, which gives the notes a warm penetration and a long decay. Against the heavy sound of the Arab oud the tembûr is lighter and more nimble; against the sharpness of the Persian setar its tone is softer and more inward. These qualities let it carry deep feeling in the spiritual chanting of the Yarsan rites, where believers regard it as a medium to the sacred realm.

The Kurdish tembûr (Tembûr) is a fretted chordophone, the original and principal form of the tembûr family, used by the Kurds. Its soundbox is pear-shaped, made from a single piece or several pieces of mulberry; the neck is walnut, with thirteen or fourteen frets set out in a semitone scale of half-equal temperament. It is strung with three metal strings, the first course doubled, and the melody is mostly played on the doubled course, the fingers of the right hand sweeping upward in turn. It is closely connected with the Yarsan (Ehli Heq) faith, and it is used in ritual in the Kurdish region and in Lorestan province in Iran, where it is regarded as sacred; it is often played with the Kurdish daf.
